content: Tanning activators are chemical agents that enhance the effects of ultraviolet (UV) radiation on human skin. These substances work by amplifying the skin's response to UV exposure, which leads to both sunburn and suntan through the same biological mechanism—direct DNA damage. This damage primarily involves the formation of thymine dimers, a type of DNA lesion caused by UVB radiation. One of the most well-known tanning activators is psoralen, a compound found in bergamot oil. Psoralen was historically included in sunscreens to promote tanning, even when the UV intensity reaching the deeper layers of the skin was reduced. However, the use of psoralen in sunscreens has been controversial due to its phototoxic and photocarcinogenic properties. In Switzerland, a ban on psoralen-containing sunscreens was introduced in 1987, but enforcement was lax for several years. In other countries, these products remained on the market until epidemiological studies revealed that users of psoralen-containing sunscreens had a fourfold increased risk of developing melanoma. As a result, these products were finally banned in 1996, more than 15 years after the carcinogenic potential of psoralen had been scientifically demonstrated. Despite the emerging evidence of psoralen's risks, sunscreens combining UVB filters with psoralen were marketed and promoted as safe or even superior alternatives to conventional sunscreens. These products were particularly recommended for individuals who had difficulty tanning. Psoralen-based tanning lotions were widely available in countries such as France, Belgium, and Greece. The mechanism of action of tanning activators involves the stimulation of melanin production in response to UVB-induced direct DNA damage. Several substances, including psoralen and coumarin, are known to increase the extent of this DNA damage, specifically by inducing the formation of thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers). For these substances to exert their effects, they must penetrate the skin, a fact that contradicts the assumptions often made by proponents of sunscreen use. Coumarin, another tanning activator, has been shown to induce thymine dimer formation and is associated with photosensitivity. As a result, patients using products containing coumarins are advised to avoid direct sunlight following treatment to minimize the risk of phototoxic reactions.
